final_answer:
The Electoral College is a system used to elect the President of the United States. Each state is allocated a number of electors equal to its total number of Senators and Representatives in Congress. During the general election, voters select a slate of electors pledged to a presidential candidate. These electors then meet in their states to formally cast votes for President. A candidate needs at least 270 electoral votes to win. 

Arguments for the system include its role in ensuring smaller states have influence, preventing urban areas from dominating the election, and maintaining a federal structure. Critics argue it can produce a president who loses the popular vote, gives disproportionate attention to swing states, and may not reflect the national will.
